entries.cbac5c964fff4a34bdf479addbc70819f0e19bf4: <div sID="gen15511" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Isa.4" sID="Isa.4"/> <div eID="gen15511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15512" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15513" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. A threatening of the paucity and scarceness of man (<reference osisRef="Isa.4.1">ver. 1</reference>), which might fitly enough have been added to the close of the foregoing chapter, to which it has a plain reference. II. A promise of the restoration of Jerusalem's peace and purity, righteousness and safety, in the days of the Messiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.4.2-Isa.4.6">ver. 2-6</reference>. Thus, in wrath, mercy is remembered, and gospel grace is a sovereign relief, in reference to the terrors of the law and the desolations made by sin.
entries.d628bc469a5ee9f05d1f6d5664792691f763bf8f: <div eID="gen15513" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15512" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Humiliation of the Daughters of Zion. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 758.)</title> <div sID="gen15514" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And in that day seven women shall take hold of one man, saying, We will eat our own bread, and wear our own apparel: only let us be called by thy name, to take away our reproach. <div eID="gen15514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15515" type="x-p"/> It was threatened (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.25">ch. iii. 25</reference>) that <hi type="italic">the mighty men should fall by the sword in war,</hi> and it was threatened as a punishment to the women that affected gaiety and a loose sort of conversation. Now here we have the effect and consequence of that great slaughter of men, 1. That though Providence has so wisely ordered that, <hi type="italic">communibus annis—on an average of years,</hi> there is nearly an equal number of males and females born into the world, yet, through the devastations made by war, there should scarcely be one man in seven left alive. As there are deaths attending the bringing forth of children, which are peculiar to the woman, who was first in transgression, so, to balance that, there are deaths peculiar to men, those by the sword in the high places of the field, which perhaps devour more than child-bed does. Here it is foretold that such multitudes of men should be cut off that there should be <hi type="italic">seven women to one man.</hi> 2. That by reason of the scarcity of men, though marriage should be kept up for the raising of recruits and the preserving of the race of mankind upon earth, yet the usual method of it should be quite altered,—that, whereas men ordinarily make their court to the women, the women should now take hold of the men, foolishly fearing (as Lot's daughters did, when they saw the ruin of Sodom and perhaps thought it reached further than it did) that in a little time there would be none left (<reference osisRef="Gen.19.31">Gen. xix. 31</reference>),—that whereas women naturally hate to come in sharers with others, seven should now, by consent, become the wives of one man,—and that whereas by the law the husband was obliged to provide food and raiment for his wife (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.10">Exod. xxi. 10</reference>), which with many would be the most powerful argument against multiplying wives, these women will be bound to support themselves; they will <hi type="italic">eat bread of their own earning, and wear apparel of their own working,</hi> and the man they court shall be at no expense upon them, only they desire to be called his wives, to <hi type="italic">take away the reproach</hi> of a single life. They are willing to be wives upon any terms, though ever so unreasonable; and perhaps the rather because in these troublesome times it would be a kindness to them to have a husband for their protector. Paul, on the contrary, thinks the single state preferable in a time of distress, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.26">1 Cor. vii. 26</reference>. It were well if this were not introduced here partly as a reflection upon the daughters of Zion, that, notwithstanding the humbling providences they were under (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.18">ch. iii. 18</reference>), they remained unhumbled, and, instead of repenting of their pride and vanity, when God was contending with them for them, all their care was to get husbands—that modesty, which is the greatest beauty of the fair sex, was forgotten, and with them the reproach of vice was nothing to the reproach of virginity, a sad symptom of the irrecoverable desolations of virtue.
entries.2c8b256a117a753bfa3c1af6ce3dd0e3528746cb: <div eID="gen15515" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Future Glory of Zion. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 758.)</title> <div sID="gen15516" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> In that day shall the branch of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the earth <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> excellent and comely for them that are escaped of Israel. <hi type="super">3</hi> And it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">that he that is</hi> left in Zion, and <hi type="italic">he that</hi> remaineth in Jerusalem, shall be called holy, <hi type="italic">even</hi> every one that is written among the living in Jerusalem: <hi type="super">4</hi> When the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion, and shall have purged the blood of Jerusalem from the midst thereof by the spirit of judgment, and by the spirit of burning. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will create upon every dwelling place of mount Zion, and upon her assemblies, a cloud and smoke by day, and the shining of a flaming fire by night: for upon all the glory <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a defence. <hi type="super">6</hi> And there shall be a tabernacle for a shadow in the daytime from the heat, and for a place of refuge, and for a covert from storm and from rain. <div eID="gen15516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15517" type="x-p"/> By the foregoing threatenings Jerusalem is brought into a very deplorable condition: every thing looks melancholy. But here the sun breaks out from behind the cloud. Many exceedingly great and precious promises we have in these verses, giving assurance of comfort which may be discerned through the troubles, and of happy days which shall come after them, and these certainly point at the kingdom of the Messiah, and the great redemption to be wrought out by him, under the figure and type of the restoration of Judah and Jerusalem by the reforming reign of Hezekiah after Ahaz and the return out of their captivity in Babylon; to both these events the passage may have some reference, but chiefly to Christ. It is here promised, as the issue of all these troubles, <div eID="gen15517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15518" type="x-p"/> I. That God will raise up a righteous branch, which shall produce fruits of righteousness (<reference osisRef="Isa.4.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">In that day,</hi> that same day, at that very time, when Jerusalem shall be destroyed and the Jewish nation extirpated and dispersed, the kingdom of the Messiah shall be set up; and then shall be the reviving of the church, when every one shall fear the utter ruin of it. <div eID="gen15518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15519" type="x-p"/> 1. Christ himself shall be exalted. He is the <hi type="italic">branch of the Lord,</hi> the man the branch; it is one of prophetical names, <hi type="italic">my servant the branch</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.8">Zech. iii. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.6.12">vi. 12</reference>), the <hi type="italic">branch of righteousness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jer. xxiii. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.33.15">xxxiii. 15</reference>), a <hi type="italic">rod out of the stem of Jesse and a branch out of his roots</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">ch. xi. 1</reference>), and this, as some think, is alluded to when he is called a <hi type="italic">Nazarene,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.2.23">Matt. ii. 23</reference>. Here he is called <hi type="italic">the branch of the Lord,</hi> because planted by his power and flourishing to his praise. The ancient Chaldee paraphrase here reads it, <hi type="italic">The Christ, or Messiah, of the Lord.</hi> He shall be the beauty, and glory, and joy. (1.) He shall himself be advanced to the joy set before him and the glory which he had with the Father before the world was. He that was a reproach of men, whose visage was marred more than any man's, is now, in the upper world, beautiful and glorious, as the sun in his strength, admired and adored by angels. (2.) He shall be beautiful and glorious in the esteem of all believers, shall gain an interest in the world, and a name among men above every name. To those that believe he is precious, he is an honour (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.7">1 Pet. ii. 7</reference>), the <hi type="italic">fairest of ten thousand</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.5.10">Cant. v. 10</reference>), and altogether glorious. Let us rejoice that he is so, and let him be so to us. <div eID="gen15519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15520" type="x-p"/> 2. His gospel shall be embraced. The success of the gospel is the fruit of the branch of the Lord; all the graces and comforts of the gospel spring from Christ. But it is called <hi type="italic">the fruit of the earth</hi> because it sprang up in this world and was calculated for the present state. And Christ compares himself to a <hi type="italic">grain of wheat,</hi> that <hi type="italic">falls into the ground and dies, and so brings forth much fruit,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.24">John xii. 24</reference>. The success of the gospel is represented by <hi type="italic">the earth's yielding her increase</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.67.6">Ps. lxvii. 6</reference>), and the planting of the Christian church is God's <hi type="italic">sowing it to himself in the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.2.23">Hos. ii. 23</reference>. We may understand it of both the persons and the things that are the products of the gospel: they shall be excellent and comely, shall appear very agreeable and be very acceptable to those that have escaped of Israel, to that remnant of the Jews which was saved from perishing with the rest in unbelief, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.5">Rom. xi. 5</reference>. Note, If Christ be precious to us, his gospel will be so and all its truths and promises—his church will be so, and all that belong to it. These are the good fruit of the earth, in comparison with which all other things are but weeds. It will be a good evidence to us that we are of the chosen remnant, distinguished from the rest that are called <hi type="italic">Israel,</hi> and marked for salvation, if we are brought to see a transcendent beauty in Christ, and in holiness, and in the saints, the excellent ones of the earth. As a type of this blessed day, Jerusalem, after Sennacherib's invasion and after the captivity in Babylon, should again flourish as a branch, and be blessed with the fruits of the earth. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.37.31-Isa.37.32">ch. xxxvii. 31, 32</reference>. <hi type="italic">The remnant shall again take root downward and bear fruit upward.</hi> And if by the fruit of the earth here we understand the good things of this life, we may observe that these have peculiar sweetness in them to the chosen remnant, who, having a covenant—right to them, have the most comfortable use of them. If the branch of the Lord be beautiful and glorious in our eyes, even the fruit of the earth also will be excellent and comely, because then we may take it as the fruit of the promise, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.16">Ps. xxxvii. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.8">1 Tim. iv. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen15520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15521" type="x-p"/> II. That God will reserve to himself a holy seed, <reference osisRef="Isa.4.3">v. 3</reference>. When the generality of those that have a place and a name in Zion and in Jerusalem shall be cut off as withered branches, by their own unbelief, yet some shall be left. Some shall remain, some shall still cleave to the church, when its property is altered and it has become Christian; for God will not quite <hi type="italic">cast off his people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.1">Rom. xi. 1</reference>. There is here and there one that is left. Now, 1. This is a remnant <hi type="italic">according to the election of grace</hi> (as the apostle speaks, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.5">Rom. xi. 5</reference>), such as are written among the living, marked in the counsel and fore-knowledge of God for life and salvation, <hi type="italic">written to life</hi> (so the word is), designed and determined for it unalterably; for "<hi type="italic">what I have written I have written.</hi>" Those that are kept alive in killing dying times were written for life in the book of divine Providence; and shall we not suppose those who are rescued from a greater death to be such as were <hi type="italic">written in the Lamb's book of life?</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.13.8">Rev. xiii. 8</reference>. As many as were <hi type="italic">ordained unto eternal life believed</hi> to <hi type="italic">the salvation of the soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.13.48">Acts xiii. 48</reference>. Note, All that were <hi type="italic">written among the living</hi> shall be found among the living, every one; for of all that were given to Christ he will lose none. 2. It is a remnant <hi type="italic">under the dominion of grace;</hi> for every one that is <hi type="italic">written among the living,</hi> and is accordingly left, shall be called <hi type="italic">holy,</hi> shall be holy, and shall be accepted of God accordingly. Those only that are holy shall be left when the <hi type="italic">Son of man shall gather out of his kingdom every thing that offends;</hi> and all that are chosen to salvation are chosen to sanctification. See <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.13">2 Thess. ii. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.4">Eph. i. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen15521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15522" type="x-p"/> III. That God will reform his church and will rectify and amend whatever is amiss in it, <reference osisRef="Isa.4.4">v. 4</reference>. Then the remnant shall be <hi type="italic">called holy, when the Lord shall have washed away their filth,</hi> washed it from among them by cutting off the wicked persons, washed it from within them by purging out the wicked thing. They shall not be called so till they are in some measure made so. Gospel times are times of reformation (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.10">Heb. ix. 10</reference>), typified by the reformation in the days of Hezekiah and that after captivity, to which this promise refers. Observe, 1. The places and persons to be reformed. Jerusalem, though the holy city, needed reformation; and, being the holy city, the reformation of that would have a good influence upon the whole kingdom. The daughters of Zion also must be reformed, the women in a particular manner, whom he had reproved, <reference osisRef="Isa.3.16">ch. iii. 16</reference>. When they were decked in their ornaments they thought themselves wondrously clean; but, being proud of them, the prophet call them their <hi type="italic">filth,</hi> for no sin is more abominable to God than pride. Or by the daughters of Zion may be meant the country towns and villages, which were related to Jerusalem as the mother-city, and which needed reformation. 2. The reformation itself. The filth shall be washed away; for wickedness is filthiness, particularly blood-shed, for which Jerusalem was infamous (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.16">2 Kings xxi. 16</reference>), and which defiles the land more than any other sin. Note, The reforming of a city is the cleansing of it. When vicious customs and fashions are suppressed, and the open practice of wickedness is restrained, the place is made clean and sweet which before was a dunghill; and this is not only for its credit and reputation among strangers, but for the comfort and health of the inhabitants themselves. 3. The author of the reformation: <hi type="italic">The Lord shall do it.</hi> Reformation-work is God's work; if any thing be done to purpose in it, it is his doing. But how? By the judgment of his providence the sinners were destroyed and consumed; but it is by the Spirit of his grace that they are reformed and converted. This is the work that is done, not by might, nor by power, but by the <hi type="italic">Spirit of the Lord of hosts</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.6">Zech. iv. 6</reference>), working both upon the sinners themselves that are to be reformed and upon magistrates, ministers, and others that are to be employed as instruments of reformation. The Spirit herein acts, (1.) As a spirit of judgment, enlightening the mind, convincing the conscience,—as a spirit of wisdom, guiding us to deal prudently, (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.13">Isa. lii. 13</reference>),—as a discerning, distinguishing, Spirit, separating between the precious and the vile. (2.) As a Spirit of burning, quickening and invigorating the afflictions, and making men zealously affected in a good work. The Spirit works as fire, <reference osisRef="Matt.3.11">Matt. iii. 11</reference>. An ardent love to Christ and souls, and a flaming zeal against sin, will carry men on with resolution in their endeavours to <hi type="italic">turn away ungodliness from Jacob.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Isa.32.15-Isa.32.16">Isa. xxxii. 15, 16</reference>. <div eID="gen15522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15523" type="x-p"/> IV. That God will protect his church, and all that belong to it (<reference osisRef="Isa.4.5-Isa.4.6">v. 5, 6</reference>); when they are purified and reformed they shall no longer lie exposed, but God will take a particular care of them. Those that are sanctified are well fortified; for God will be to them a guide and a guard. <div eID="gen15523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15524" type="x-p"/> 1. Their tabernacles shall be defended, <reference osisRef="Isa.4.5">v. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen15524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15525" type="x-p"/> (1.) This writ of protection refers to, [1.] Their dwelling places, the tabernacles of their rest, their own houses, where they worship God alone, and with their families. That blessing which is upon the <hi type="italic">habitation of the just</hi> shall be a protection to it, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.33">Prov. iii. 33</reference>. In the <hi type="italic">tabernacles of the righteous</hi> shall the <hi type="italic">voice of rejoicing and salvation be,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.118.15">Ps. cxviii. 15</reference>. Note, God takes particular cognizance and care of the dwelling-places of his people, of every one of them, the poorest cottage as well as the statliest palace. When iniquity is <hi type="italic">put far from the tabernacle</hi> the Almighty shall be its defence, <reference osisRef="Job.23.23">Job xxiii. 23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.23.26">26</reference>. [2.] Their assemblies or tabernacles of meeting for religious worship. No mention is made of the temple, for the promise points at a time when not one stone of that shall be left upon another; but all the congregations of Christians, though but two or three met together in Christ's name, shall be taken under the special protection of heaven; they shall be no more scattered, no more disturbed, nor shall <hi type="italic">any weapon formed against them prosper.</hi> Note, we ought to reckon it a great mercy if we have liberty to worship God in public, free from the alarms of the sword of war or persecution. <div eID="gen15525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15526" type="x-p"/> (2.) This writ of protection is drawn up, [1.] In a similitude taken from the safety of the camp of Israel when they marched through the wilderness. God will give to the Christian church as real proofs, though not so sensible, of his care of them, as he then gave to Israel. The Lord will again <hi type="italic">create a cloud and smoke by day,</hi> to screen them from the scorching heat of the sun, and the <hi type="italic">shining of a flaming fire by night,</hi> to enlighten and warm the air, which in the night is cold and dark. See <reference osisRef="Exod.13.21">Exod. xiii. 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.9.19">Neh. ix. 19</reference>. This pillar of cloud and fire interposed between the Israelites and the Egyptians, <reference osisRef="Exod.14.20">Exod. xiv. 20</reference>. Note, Though miracles have ceased, yet God is the same to the New-Testament church that he was to Israel of old; the very same yesterday, to-day, and for ever. [2.] In a similitude taken from the outside cover of rams' skins and badgers' skins that was upon the curtains of the tabernacle, as if every dwelling place of Mount Zion and every assembly were as dear to God as that tabernacle was: <hi type="italic">Upon all the glory shall be a defense,</hi> to save it from wind and weather. Note, The church on earth has its glory. Gospel truths and ordinances, the scriptures and the ministry, are the church's glory; and upon all this glory there is a defence, and ever shall be, for the <hi type="italic">gates of hell shall not prevail against the church.</hi> If God himself be the glory in the midst of it, he will himself be a wall of fire around about it, impenetrable and impregnable. Grace in the soul is the glory of it, and those that have it are <hi type="italic">kept by the power of God</hi> as in a strong-hold, <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.5">1 Pet. i. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen15526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15527" type="x-p"/> 2. Their tabernacle shall be a defence to them, <reference osisRef="Isa.4.6">v. 6</reference>. God's tabernacle was a pavilion to the saints (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.5">Ps. xxvii. 5</reference>); but, when that is taken down, they shall not want a covert: the divine power and goodness shall be a tabernacle to all the saints. God himself will be their hiding-place (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.7">Ps. xxxii. 7</reference>); they shall be at home in him, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.9">Ps. xci. 9</reference>. He will himself be to them as the <hi type="italic">shadow of a great rock</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.2">ch. xxxii. 2</reference>) and <hi type="italic">his name a strong tower,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.10">Prov. xviii. 10</reference>. He will be not only a shadow from the heat in the daytime, but a covert from storm and rain. Note, In this world we must expect change of weather and all the inconveniences that attend it; we shall meet with storm and rain in this lower region, and at other times the heat of the day no less burdensome; but God is a refuge to his people in all weathers.  <chapter eID="Isa.4"/> <div eID="gen15527" type="x-p"/>

entries.d4ffedf190855a16272103c2d45d0f1346c6b9f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8385"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <div sID="gen13426" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.4.1-Isa.4.6">Is 4:1-6</reference>.<div eID="gen13426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13427" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that day--</hi>the calamitous period described in previous chapter.<div eID="gen13427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13428" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seven--</hi>indefinite number among the Jews. So many men would be slain, that there would be very many more women than men; for example, seven women, contrary to their natural bashfulness, would sue to (equivalent to "take hold of," <reference osisRef="Isa.3.6">Is 3:6</reference>) one man to marry them.<div eID="gen13428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13429" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eat ... own bread--</hi>foregoing the privileges, which the law (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.10">Ex 21:10</reference>) gives to wives, when a man has more than one.<div eID="gen13429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13430" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reproach--</hi>of being unwedded and childless; especially felt among the Jews, who were looking for "the seed of the woman," Jesus Christ, described in <reference osisRef="Isa.4.2">Is 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.54.1">Is 54:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.54.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.25">Lu 1:25</reference>.<div eID="gen13430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13431" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8385"/>2. In contrast to those on whom vengeance falls, there is a manifestation of Jesus Christ to the "escaped of Israel" in His characteristic attributes, beauty and glory, typified in Aaron's garments (<reference osisRef="Exod.28.2">Ex 28:2</reference>). Their sanctification is promised as the fruit of their being "written" in the book of life by sovereign love (<reference osisRef="Isa.4.3">Is 4:3</reference>); the means of it are the "spirit of judgment" and that of "burning" (<reference osisRef="Isa.4.4">Is 4:4</reference>). Their "defense" by the special presence of Jesus Christ is promised (<reference osisRef="Isa.4.5">Is 4:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.4.6">6</reference>).<div eID="gen13431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13432" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">branch--</hi>the sprout of Jehovah. Messiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jr 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.33.15">33:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.3.8">Zec 3:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.6.12">6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.78">Lu 1:78</reference>, Margin). The parallel clause does not, as Maurer objects, oppose this; for "fruit of the earth" answers to "branch"; He shall not be a dry, but a fruit-bearing branch (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.6">Is 27:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.23-Ezek.34.27">Eze 34:23-27</reference>). He is "of the earth" in His birth and death, while He is also "of the Lord" (Jehovah) (<reference osisRef="John.12.24">Joh 12:24</reference>). His name, "the Branch," chiefly regards His descent from David, when the family was low and reduced (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.4">Lu 2:4</reference>, 7, 24); a sprout with more than David's glory, springing as from a decayed tree (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Is 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.53.2">53:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.16">Re 22:16</reference>).<div eID="gen13432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13433" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">excellent--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Heb.1.4">He 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.6">8:6</reference>).<div eID="gen13433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13434" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">comely--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Song.5.15">So 5:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.5.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.14">Eze 16:14</reference>).<div eID="gen13434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13435" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">escaped of Israel--</hi>the elect remnant (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.5">Ro 11:5</reference>); (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.1">1</reference>) in the return from Babylon; (2) in the escape from Jerusalem's destruction under Titus; (3) in the still future assault on Jerusalem, and deliverance of "the third part"; events mutually analogous, like concentric circles (Zec 12:2-10; 13:8, 9, &c.; 14:2; <reference osisRef="Ezek.39.23-Ezek.39.29">Eze 39:23-29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.3.1-Joel.3.21">Joe 3:1-21</reference>). <div eID="gen13435" type="x-p"/>
entries.17a6c565b7f2a6e0032240e97a84f478f55474b1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8386"/><div sID="gen13436" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8386"/><hi type="bold">3. left in Zion--</hi>equivalent to the "escaped of Israel" (<reference osisRef="Isa.4.2">Is 4:2</reference>).<div eID="gen13436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13437" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall be called--</hi>shall be (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>).<div eID="gen13437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13438" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">holy--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.52.1">Is 52:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.21">60:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.27">Re 21:27</reference>).<div eID="gen13438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13439" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">written--</hi>in the book of life, antitypically (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.3">Php 4:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.5">Re 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.17.8">17:8</reference>). Primarily, in the register kept of Israel's families and tribes.<div eID="gen13439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13440" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">living--</hi>not "blotted out" from the registry, as dead; but written there as among the "escaped of Israel" (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.1">Da 12:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.9">Eze 13:9</reference>). To the elect of Israel, rather than the saved in general, the special reference is here (<reference osisRef="Joel.3.17">Joe 3:17</reference>). <div eID="gen13440" type="x-p"/>
entries.d69f8c98116bf5acd5e0a0447579a019fbb1cda1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8387"/><div sID="gen13441" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8387"/><hi type="bold">4. When--</hi>that is, After.<div eID="gen13441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13442" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">washed--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Zech.13.1">Zec 13:1</reference>).<div eID="gen13442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13443" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">filth--</hi>moral (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.21-Isa.1.25">Is 1:21-25</reference>).<div eID="gen13443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13444" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">daughters of Zion--</hi>same as in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.16">Is 3:16</reference>.<div eID="gen13444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13445" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">purged--</hi>purified by judgments; destroying the ungodly, correcting and refining the godly.<div eID="gen13445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13446" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blood--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.1.15">Is 1:15</reference>).<div eID="gen13446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13447" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spirit--</hi>Whatever God does in the universe, He does by His Spirit, "without the hand" of man (<reference osisRef="Job.34.20">Job 34:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.30">Psa 104:30</reference>). Here He is represented using His power as Judge.<div eID="gen13447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13448" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">burning--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Matt.3.11">Mt 3:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.3.12">12</reference>). The same Holy Ghost, who sanctifies believers by the fire of affliction (Mal 3:2, 3), dooms unbelievers to the fire of perdition (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.13-1Cor.3.15">1Co 3:13-15</reference>). <div eID="gen13448" type="x-p"/>
entries.0331caa06ca8fc50f9512ead6001998bb52f6ecf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8388"/><div sID="gen13449" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8388"/><hi type="bold">5. create--</hi>The "new creation" needs as much God's creative omnipotence, as the material creation (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6">2Co 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.10">Ep 2:10</reference>). So it shall be in the case of the Holy Jerusalem to come (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.17">Is 65:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.18">18</reference>).<div eID="gen13449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13450" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon--</hi>The pillar of cloud stood over the tabernacle, as symbol of God's favor and presence (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.21">Ex 13:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.22">22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1">Psa 91:1</reference>). Both on individual families ("every dwelling") and on the general sacred "assemblies" (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.2">Le 23:2</reference>). The "cloud" became a "fire" by night in order to be seen by the Lord's people.<div eID="gen13450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13451" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon all the glory--</hi>"upon the glorious whole"; namely, the Lord's people and sanctuary [Maurer]. May it not mean, "Upon whatever the glory (the Shekinah spoken of in the previous clause) shall rest, there shall be a defense." The symbol of His presence shall ensure also safety. So it was to Israel against the Egyptians at the Red Sea (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.19">Ex 14:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.14.20">20</reference>). So it shall be to literal Jerusalem hereafter (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.5">Zec 2:5</reference>). Also to the Church, the spiritual "Zion" (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.18">Is 32:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.15-Isa.33.17">33:15-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.22">He 12:22</reference>).<div eID="gen13451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13452" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tabernacle--</hi>Christ's body (<reference osisRef="John.1.14">Joh 1:14</reference>). "The word 'tabernacled' (Greek for 'dwelt') among us" (<reference osisRef="John.2.21">Joh 2:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.8.2">He 8:2</reference>). It is a "shadow from the heat" and "refuge from the storm" of divine wrath against man's sins (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.4">Is 25:4</reference>). Heat and storms are violent in the East; so that a portable tent is a needful part of a traveller's outfit. Such shall be God's wrath hereafter, from which the "escaped of Israel" shall be sheltered by Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.20">Is 26:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.2">32:2</reference>).<div eID="gen13452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13453" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">covert--</hi>answering to "defense" (<reference osisRef="Isa.4.5">Is 4:5</reference>). The Hebrew for defense in <reference osisRef="Isa.4.5">Is 4:5</reference>, is "covering"; the lid of the ark or mercy seat was named from the same Hebrew word, caphar; the propitiatory; for it, being sprinkled with blood by the high priest once a year, on the day of atonement, covered the people typically from wrath. Jesus Christ is the true Mercy Seat, on whom the Shekinah rested, the propitiatory, or atonement, beneath whom the law is kept, as it was literally within the ark, and man is covered from the storm. The redeemed Israel shall also be, by union with Him, a tabernacle for God's glory, which, unlike that in the wilderness, shall not be taken down (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.20">Is 38:20</reference>). <chapter eID="Isa.4"/>

entries.fd66660796695d2bcb3fa961e643059d95ac38eb: <div eID="gen26660" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen26661" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26662" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26662" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26661" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26663" type="x-p"/> The havoc occasioned by war, and those other calamities which the prophet had been describing in the preceding chapter, are represented as so terribly great that seven women should be left to one man, <reference osisRef="Isa.4.1">Isa 4:1</reference>. Great blessedness of the remnant that shall be accounted worthy to escape these judgments, <reference osisRef="Isa.4.2-Isa.4.4">Isa 4:2-4</reference>. The privileges of the Gospel set forth by allusions to the glory and pomp of the Mosaic dispensation, <reference osisRef="Isa.4.5">Isa 4:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.4.6">Isa 4:6</reference>. <div eID="gen26663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26664" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen26664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26665" type="x-p"/> And seven women - The division of the chapters has interrupted the prophet's discourse, and broken it off almost in the midst of the sentence. "The numbers slain in battle shall be so great, that seven women shall be left to one man." The prophet has described the greatness of this distress by images and adjuncts the most expressive and forcible. The young women, contrary to their natural modesty, shall become suitors to the men: they will take hold of them, and use the most pressing importunity to be married. In spite of the natural suggestions of jealousy, they will be content with a share only of the rights of marriage in common with several others; and that on hard conditions, renouncing the legal demands of the wife on the husband, (see <reference osisRef="Exo.21.10">Exo 21:10</reference>), and begging only the name and credit of wedlock, and to be freed from the reproach of celibacy. See <reference osisRef="Isa.54.4">Isa 54:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.54.5">Isa 54:5</reference>. Like Marcia, on a different occasion, and in other circumstances: - <div eID="gen26665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26666" type="x-p"/> Da tantum nomen inane <div eID="gen26666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26667" type="x-p"/> Connubii: liceat tumulo scripsisse, Catonis Marcia. <div eID="gen26667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26668" type="x-p"/> Lucan, 2:342. "This happened," says Kimchi, "in the days of Ahaz, when Pekah the son of Remaliah slew in Judea one hundred and twenty thousand men in one day; see <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.6">2Chr 18:6</reference>. The widows which were left were so numerous that the prophet said, 'They are multiplied beyond the sand of the sea,'" <reference osisRef="Jer.15.8">Jer 15:8</reference>. <div eID="gen26668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26669" type="x-p"/> In that day - These words are omitted in the Septuagint, and MSS.
entries.1187b4c5f4e5b06682e0e8efb9d1954e5a14141a: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen26669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26670" type="x-p"/> The branch of the Lord "the branch of Jehovah" - The Messiah of Jehovah, says the Chaldee. And Kimchi says, The Messiah, the Son of David. The branch is an appropriate title of the Messiah; and the fruit of the land means the great Person to spring from the house of Judah, and is only a parallel expression signifying the same; or perhaps the blessings consequent upon the redemption procured by him. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.45.8">Isa 45:8</reference> (note), where the same great event is set forth under similar images, and see the note there. <div eID="gen26670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26671" type="x-p"/> Them that are escaped of Israel "the escaped of the house of Israel" - A MS. has בית ישראל beith yisrael, the house of Israel.
entries.4af30bf3bc2e436374688bfe85d6aa660f3ea997: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen26671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26672" type="x-p"/> Written among the living - That is, whose name stands in the enrolment or register of the people; or every man living, who is a citizen of Jerusalem. See <reference osisRef="Eze.13.9">Eze 13:9</reference>, where, "they shall not be written in the writing of the house of Israel," is the same with what immediately goes before, "they shall not be in the assembly of my people." Compare <reference osisRef="Psa.69.28">Psa 69:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.87.6">Psa 87:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exo.32.32">Exo 32:32</reference>. To number and register the people was agreeable to the law of Moses, and probably was always practiced; being, in sound policy, useful, and even necessary. David's design of numbering the people was of another kind; it was to enroll them for his army. Michaelis Mosaisches Recht, Part iii., p. 227. See also his Dissert. de Censibus Hebraeorum.
entries.13f56405e28eef52984763475a46e8a5c81461e7: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen26672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26673" type="x-p"/> The spirit of burning - Means the fire of God's wrath, by which he will prove and purify his people; gathering them into his furnace, in order to separate the dross from the silver, the bad from the good. The severity of God's judgments, the fiery trial of his servants, Ezekiel (<reference osisRef="Eze.22.18-Eze.22.22">Eze 22:18-22</reference>) has set forth at large, after his manner, with great boldness of imagery and force of expression. God threatens to gather them into the midst of Jerusalem, as into the furnace; to blow the fire upon them, and to melt them. Malachi, <reference osisRef="Mal.3.2">Mal 3:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mal.3.3">Mal 3:3</reference>, treats the same subject, and represents the same event, under the like images: - "But who may abide the day of his coming? <div eID="gen26673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26674" type="x-p"/> And who shall stand when he appeareth? <div eID="gen26674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26675" type="x-p"/> For he is like the fire of the refiner, <div eID="gen26675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26676" type="x-p"/> And like the soap of the fullers. <div eID="gen26676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26677" type="x-p"/> And he shall sit refining and purifying the silver; <div eID="gen26677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26678" type="x-p"/> And he shall purify the sons of Levi; <div eID="gen26678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26679" type="x-p"/> And cleanse them like gold, and like silver; <div eID="gen26679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26680" type="x-p"/> That they may be Jehovah's ministers, <div eID="gen26680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26681" type="x-p"/> Presenting unto him an offering in righteousness." <div eID="gen26681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26682" type="x-p"/> This is an allusion to a chemist purifying metals. He first judges of the state of the ore or adulterated metal. Secondly, he kindles the proper degree of fire, and applies the requisite test; and thus separates the precious from the vile.
entries.da858878569509a639b57d39222b8ddb00815b93: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen26682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26683" type="x-p"/> And the Lord will create - One MS., the Septuagint, and the Arabic, have יביא yabi, He shall bring: the cloud already exists; the Lord will bring it over. This is a blessed promise of the presence of God in all the assemblies of his people. <div eID="gen26683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26684" type="x-p"/> Every dwelling place "the station" - The Hebrew text has, every station: but four MSS. (one ancient) omit כל col, all; very rightly, as it should seem: for the station was Mount Zion itself, and no other. See <reference osisRef="Exo.15.17">Exo 15:17</reference>. And the Septuagint, Arabic, and MSS., add the same word כל col, before מקראה mikraeha, probably right: the word has only changed its place by mistake. מקראיה mikrayeh, "the place where they were gathered together in their holy assemblies," says Sal ben Melech. But twenty-five of Kennicott's MSS., and twenty-two of De Rossi's fifty-three editions, besides the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic, have the word in the plural number. <div eID="gen26684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26685" type="x-p"/> A cloud and smoke by day - This is a manifest allusion to the pillar of a cloud and of fire which attended the Israelites in their passage out of Egypt, and to the glory that rested on the tabernacle, <reference osisRef="Exo.13.21">Exo 13:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exo.40.38">Exo 40:38</reference>. The prophet Zechariah, <reference osisRef="Zac.2.5">Zac 2:5</reference>, applies the same image to the same purpose: - "And I will be unto her a wall of fire round about; <div eID="gen26685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26686" type="x-p"/> And a glory will I be in the midst of her." <div eID="gen26686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26687" type="x-p"/> That is, the visible presence of God shall protect her. Which explains the conclusion of this verse of Isaiah; where the makkaph between כל col, and כבוד cabod, connecting the two words in construction, which ought not to be connected, has thrown an obscurity upon the sentence, and misled most of the translators. <div eID="gen26687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26688" type="x-p"/> For upon all the glory shall be a defense - Whatever God creates, he must uphold, or it will fail, Every degree of grace brings with it a degree of power to maintain itself in the soul.
entries.902e4d931b3eccd756c7ac3271d23cd6d109b0e8: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen26688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26689" type="x-p"/> A tabernacle - In countries subject to violent tempests, as well as to intolerable heat, a portable tent is a necessary part of a traveller's baggage, for defense and shelter. And to such tents the words of the text make evident allusion. They are to be met with in every part of Arabia and Egypt, and in various other places in the East.  <chapter eID="Isa.4"/> <div eID="gen26689" type="x-p"/>

entries.3cbe18d58508448125480fc2b786253ca1e84a12: <reference osisRef="Isa.4.1">Isa 4:1</reference> <div eID="gen12844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12845" type="x-p"/> When war shall thus unsparingly have swept away the men of Zion, a most unnatural effect will ensue, namely, that women will go in search of husbands, and not men in search of wives. <hi type="italic">“And seven women lay hold of one man in that day, saying, We will eat our won bread, and wear our own clothes; only let thy name be named upon us, take away our reproach.”</hi> The division of the chapters is a wrong one here, as this v. is the closing v. of the prophecy against the women, and the closing portion of the whole address does not begin till Isa 4:2. The present pride of the daughters of Zion, every one of whom now thought herself the greatest as the wife of such and such a man, and for whom many men were now the suitors, would end in this unnatural self-humiliation, that seven of them would offer themselves to the same man, the first man who presented himself, and even renounce the ordinary legal claim upon their husband for clothing and food (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.10">Exo 21:10</reference>). It would be quite sufficient for them to be allowed to bear his name (“let thy name be named <hi type="italic">upon</hi> us:” the name is put upon the thing named, as giving it its distinctness and character), if he would only take away their reproach (namely, the reproach of being unmarried, <reference osisRef="Isa.54.4">Isa 54:4</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.30.23">Gen 30:23</reference>, of being childless) by letting them be called his wives. The number <hi type="italic">seven</hi> (seven women to one man) may be explained on the ground that there is a bad seven as well as a holy one (e.g., <reference osisRef="Matt.12.45">Mat 12:45</reference>). <div eID="gen12845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12846" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Isa.4.1">Isa 4:1</reference> the threat denounced against the women of Jerusalem is brought to a close. It is the side-piece to the threat denounced against the national rulers. And these two scenes of judgment were only parts of the general judgment about to fall upon Jerusalem and Judah, as a state or national community. And this again was merely a portion, viz., the central group of the picture of a far more comprehensive judgment, which was about to fall upon everything lofty and exalted on the earth. Jerusalem, therefore, stands here as the centre and focus of the great judgment-day. It was in Jerusalem that the ungodly glory which was ripe for judgment was concentrated; and it was in Jerusalem also that the light of the true and final glory would concentrate itself. To this promise, with which the address returns to its starting-point, the prophet now passes on without any further introduction. In fact it needed no introduction, for the judgment in itself was the medium of salvation. When Jerusalem was judged, it would be sifted; and by being sifted, it would be rescued, pardoned, glorified. The prophet proceeds in this sense to speak of what would happen in that day, and describes the one great day of God at the end of time (not a day of four-and-twenty hours any more than the seven days of creation were), according to its general character, as opening with judgment, but issuing in salvation.
entries.8d1da59c26c3cfcf2478404690126f15f0dd21eb: <reference osisRef="Isa.4.2">Isa 4:2</reference> <hi type="italic">“In that day will the sprout of Jehovah become an ornament and glory, and the fruit of the land pride and splendour for the redeemed of Israel.”</hi> The four epithets of glory, which are here grouped in pairs, strengthen our expectation, that now that the mass of Israel has been swept away, together with the objects of its worthless pride, we shall find a description of what will become an object of well-grounded pride to the “escaped of Israel,” i.e., to the remnant that has survived the judgment, and been saved from destruction. But with this interpretation of the promise it is impossible that it can be the church of the future itself, which is here called the <hi type="italic">“sprout of Jehovah”</hi> and <hi type="italic">“fruit of the land,”</hi> as Luzzatto and Malbim suppose; and equally impossible, with such an antithesis between what is promised and what is abolished, that the “sprout of Jehovah” and “fruit of the earth” should signify the harvest blessings bestowed by Jehovah, or the rich produce of the land. For although the expression <hi type="italic">zemach</hi> <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> (sprout of Jehovah) may unquestionably be used to signify this, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.2.9">Gen 2:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.104.14">Psa 104:14</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.61.11">Isa 61:11</reference>), and fruitfulness of the land is a standing accompaniment of the eschatological promises (e.g., Isa 30:23., compare the conclusion of Joel and Amos), and it was also foretold that the fruitful fields of Israel would become a glory in the sight of the nations (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.29">Eze 34:29</reference>; Mal 3:12; cf., <reference osisRef="Joel.2.17">Joe 2:17</reference>); yet this earthly material good, of which, moreover, there was no lack in the time of Uzziah and Jotham, was altogether unsuitable to set forth such a contrast as would surpass and outshine the worldly glory existing before. But even granting what Hofmann adduces in support of this view - namely, that the natural God-given blessings of the field do form a fitting antithesis to the studied works of art of which men had hitherto been proud - there is still truth in the remark of Rosenmüller, that “the magnificence of the whole passage is at variance with such an interpretation.” Only compare <reference osisRef="Isa.28.5">Isa 28:5</reference>, where Jehovah Himself is described in the same manner, as the glory and ornament of the remnant of Israel. But if the “sprout of Jehovah” is neither the redeemed remnant itself, nor the fruit of the field, it must be the name of the Messiah. And it is in this sense that it has been understood by the Targum, and by such modern commentators as Rosenmüller, Hengstenberg, Steudel, Umbreit, Caspari, Drechsler, and others. The great King of the future is called <hi type="italic">zemach</hi>, ἀνατολή in the sense of <reference osisRef="Heb.7.14">Heb 7:14</reference>, viz., as a shoot springing out of the human, Davidic, earthly soil - a shoot which Jehovah had planted in the earth, and would cause to break through and spring forth as the pride of His congregation, which was waiting for this heavenly child. It is He again who is designated in the parallel clause as the <hi type="italic">“fruit of the land”</hi> (or lit., fruit of the earth), as being the fruit which the land of Israel, and consequently the earth itself, would produce, just as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.5">Eze 17:5</reference> Zedekiah is called a “seed of the earth.” The reasons already adduced to show that “the sprout of Jehovah” cannot refer to the blessings of the field, apply with equal force to “the fruit of the earth.” This also relates to the Messiah Himself, regarded as the fruit in which all the growth and bloom of this earthly history would eventually reach its promised and divinely appointed conclusion. The use of this double epithet to denote “the coming One” can only be accounted for, without anticipating the New Testament standpoint,<note placement="foot">From a New Testament point of view we might say that the “sprout of Jehovah” or “fruit of the earth” was the grain of wheat which redeeming love sowed in the earth on Good Friday; the grain of wheat which began to break through the ground and grow towards heaven on Easter Sunday; the grain of wheat whose golden blade ascended heavenwards on Ascension Day; the grain of wheat whose myriad-fold ear bent down to the earth on the day of Pentecost, and poured out the grains, from which the holy church not only was born, but still continues to be born. But such thoughts as these lie outside the historico-grammatical meaning.</note> from the desire to depict His double-sided origin. He would come, on the one hand, from <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>; but, on the other hand, from <hi type="italic">the earth</hi>, inasmuch as He would spring from Israel. We have here the passage, on the basis of which <hi type="italic">zemach</hi> (the sprout of “Branch”) was adopted by Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jer 23:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.33.15">Jer 33:15</reference>) and Zechariah (Zec 3:8; Zec 6:12) as a proper name for the Messiah, and upon which Matthew, by combining this proper name <hi type="italic">zemach</hi> (sprout) with <hi type="italic">nezer</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Isa 11:1</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.53.2">Isa 53:2</reference>), rests his affirmation, that according to the Old Testament prophecies the future Messiah was to be called a Nazarene. It is undoubtedly strange that this epithet should be introduced so entirely without preparation even by Isaiah, who coined it first. In fact, the whole passage relating to the Messiah stands quite alone in this cycle of prophecies in chapters 1-6. But the book of Isaiah is a complete and connected work. What the prophet indicates merely in outline here, he carries out more fully in the cycle of prophecies which follows in chapters 7-12; and there the enigma, which he leaves as an enigma in the passage before us, receives the fullest solution. Without dwelling any further upon the <hi type="italic">man</hi> of the future, described in this enigmatically symbolical way, the prophet hurries on to a more precise description of the <hi type="italic">church</hi> of the future.
entries.abcd959ad42e3a63a5d5e072963184ce17fb0edc: <reference osisRef="Isa.4.3">Isa 4:3</reference> <hi type="italic">“And it will come to pass, whoever is left in Zion and remains in Jerusalem, holy will he be called, all who are written down for life in Jerusalem.”</hi> The leading emphasis of the whole v. rests upon <hi type="italic">kadosh</hi> (holy). Whereas formerly in Jerusalem persons had been distinguished according to their rank and condition, without any regard to their moral worth (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.1-Isa.3.3">Isa 3:1-3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.3.10-Isa.3.11">Isa 3:10-11</reference>; cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.32.5">Isa 32:5</reference>); so the name <hi type="italic">kadosh</hi> (holy) would now be the one chief name of honour, and would be given to every individual, inasmuch as the national calling of Israel would now be realized in the persons of all (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">Exo 19:6</reference>, etc.). Consequently the expression <hi type="italic">“he shall be called”</hi> is not exactly equivalent to “he shall be,” but rather presupposes the latter, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.26">Isa 1:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.6">Isa 61:6</reference>; Isa 62:4. The term <hi type="italic">kadosh</hi> denotes that which is withdrawn from the world, or separated from it. The church of the saints or holy ones, which now inhabits Jerusalem, is what has been left from the smelting; and their holiness is the result of washing. הנוּתר is interchanged with נהנּשׁאר. The latter, as Papenheim has shown in his Hebrew synonyms, involves the idea of intention, viz., “that which has been left behind;” the former merely expresses the fact, viz., that which remains. The character of this “remnant of grace,” and the number of members of which it would consist, are shown in the apposition contained in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.4.3">Isa 4:3</reference></hi>. This apposition means something more than those who are entered as living in Jerusalem, i.e., the population of Jerusalem as entered in the city register (Hofmann); for the verb with <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> does not mean merely to enter as a certain thing, but (like the same verb with the accusative in <reference osisRef="Jer.22.30">Jer 22:30</reference>) to enter as intended for a certain purpose. The expression להיּים may either be taken as a noun, viz., “to life” (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.2">Dan 12:2</reference>), or as an adjective, “to the living” (a meaning which is quite as tenable; cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.69.29">Psa 69:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.29">1Sa 25:29</reference>). In either case the notion of predestination is implied, and the assumption of the existence of a divine “book of life” (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.32-Exod.32.33">Exo 32:32-33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.1">Dan 12:1</reference>; cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.139.16">Psa 139:16</reference>); so that the idea is the same as that of <reference osisRef="Acts.13.48">Act 13:48</reference> : “As many as were ordained to eternal life.” The reference here is to persons who were entered in the book of God, on account of the good kernel of faith within them, as those who should become partakers of the life in the new Jerusalem, and should therefore be spared in the midst of the judgment of sifting in accordance with this divine purpose of grace. For it was only through the judgment setting this kernel of faith at liberty, that such a holy community as is described in the protasis which comes afterwards, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.63.6-Ps.63.7">Psa 63:6-7</reference>, could possibly arise.
entries.58b544b6e6d78c346f88aa72672a9e3ea8b76905: <reference osisRef="Isa.4.4">Isa 4:4</reference> <hi type="italic">“When the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion, and shall have purged away the bloodguiltinesses of Jerusalem from the midst thereof, by the spirit of judgment and by the spirit of sifting.”</hi> <hi type="italic">“When,”</hi> followed by a preterite (equivalent to a <hi type="italic">fut. exact</hi>. as in <reference osisRef="Isa.24.13">Isa 24:13</reference>; Ges. §126, 5), introduces the circumstance, whose previous occurrence would be the condition of all the rest. The force of the future <hi type="italic">yâdiach</hi> (“shall have purged”) is regulated by that of the preterite <hi type="italic">râchatz</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.6.11">Isa 6:11</reference>; for although, when regarded simply by itself, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.12">Isa 10:12</reference>, the future tense may suggest the idea of a future prefect, it cannot have the force of such a future. The double purification answers to the two scenes of judgment described in chapter 3. The filth of the daughters of Zion is the moral pollution hidden under their vain and coquettish finery; and the murderous deeds of Jerusalem are the acts of judicial murder committed by its rulers upon the poor and innocent. This filth and these spots of blood the Sovereign Ruler washes and purges away (see <reference osisRef="2Chr.4.6">2Ch 4:6</reference>), by causing His spirit or His breath to burst in upon all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, both male and female. This breath is called “the spirit of judgment,” because it punishes evil; and “the spirit of sifting,” inasmuch as it sweeps or cleans it away. בּער is to be explained, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.6.13">Isa 6:13</reference>, in accordance with <reference osisRef="Deut.13.6">Deu 13:6</reference> (<reference osisRef="Deut.13.5">5</reference>, Eng. Ver.; “put the evil away”) and other passages, such especially as <reference osisRef="Isa.19.13">Isa 19:13</reference>; Isa 21:9. The rendering given in the Septuagint and Vulgate, viz., “in the spirit of burning,” is founded upon the radical meaning of the verb, which signifies literally to burn up, and hence to clear away or destroy (see <hi type="italic">Comm. on Job</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Job.31.12">Job 31:12</reference>, Eng. Tr.). Nevertheless, “burning” in connection with judgment is not definite enough, since every manifestation of divine judgment is a manifestation of fire; but it is not every judgment that has connected with it what is here implied - namely, the salutary object of burning away or, in other words, of winnowing. The “spirit” is in both instances the Spirit of God which pervades the world, not only generating and sustaining life, but also at times destroying and sifting (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.27-Isa.30.28">Isa 30:27-28</reference>), as it does in the case before us, in which the imperishable glory described in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.5">Isa 3:5</reference> is so prepared.
entries.e85dbb1973006c3c5c048fa904b88c1054ec1d73: <reference osisRef="Isa.4.5">Isa 4:5</reference> <hi type="italic">“And Jehovah creates over every spot of Mount Zion, and over its festal assemblies, a cloud by day, and smoke, and the shining of flaming fire by night: for over all the glory comes a canopy.”</hi> Just as Jehovah guided and shielded Israel in the days of the redemption from Egypt in a smoke-cloud by day and a fire-cloud by night, which either moved in front like a pillar, or floated above them as a roof (Num 14:14, etc.), the perpetuation of His presence at Sinai (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.9">Exo 19:9</reference>, Exo 19:16.); so would Jehovah in like manner shield the Israel of the final redemption, which would no longer need the pillar of cloud since its wanderings would be over, but only the cloudy covering; and such a covering Jehovah would create, as the praet. consec. וּברא) (“and He creates”) distinctly affirms. The verb <hi type="italic">bârâh</hi> always denotes a divine and miraculous production, having its commencement in time; for even the natural is also supernatural in its first institution by God. In the case before us, however, the reference is to a fresh manifestation of His gracious presence, exalted above the present course of nature. This manifestation would consist by day in “a cloud,” and as the <hi type="italic">hendiadys</hi> “cloud and smoke” (i.e., cloud in form and smoke in substance) distinctly affirms, a smoke-cloud, not a watery cloud, like those which ordinarily cover the sky; and by night in a fiery splendour, not merely a lingering fiery splendour like that of the evening sky, but, as the words clearly indicate, a flaming brightness (<hi type="italic">lehâbâh</hi> ), and therefore real and living fire. The purpose of the cloud would not only be to overshadow, but also to serve as a wall of defence against opposing influences;<note placement="foot">The cloud derived its name, <hi type="italic">‛ânân</hi>, not from the idea of covering, but from that of coming to meet one. The clouds come towards the man who gazes at them, inserting themselves between him and the sky, and thus forcing themselves upon his notice instead of the sky; hence the visible outer side of the vault of heaven is also called <hi type="italic">‛anan</hi> (plur. <hi type="italic">‛anân</hi>), just as the same word is used to denote the outermost portion of the branches or foliage of a tree which is the first to strike the eye (in contradistinction to the inner portions, which are not so easily seen, seven if visible at all).</note> and the fire would not only give light, but by flaming and flashing would ward off hostile powers. But, above all, the cloud and fire were intended as signs of the nearness of God, and His satisfaction. In the most glorious times of the temple a smoke-cloud of this kind filled the Holy of holies; and there was only one occasion - namely, at the dedication of Solomon’s temple - on which it filled the whole building (1Ki 8:10); but now the cloud, the smoke of which, moreover, would be turned at night into flaming fire, would extend over every spot (<hi type="italic">mâcōn</hi>, a more poetical word for <hi type="italic">mâkōm</hi>) of Mount Zion, and over the festal assemblies thereon. The whole mountain would thus become a Holy of holies. It would be holy not only as being the dwelling-place of Jehovah, but as the gathering-place of a community of saints. <hi type="italic">“Her assemblies”</hi> (<hi type="italic">mikrâehâ</hi>) points back to Zion, and is a plural written defectively (at least in our editions),<note placement="foot">Such codices and ancient editions as Soncino (1488), Brescia (1494), and many others, have the word with the <hi type="italic">yod</hi> of the plural.</note>  - as, for example, in Jer 19:8. There is no necessity to take this noun in the sense of “meeting halls” (a meaning which it never has anywhere else), as Gesenius, Ewald, Hitzig, and others have done, since it may also signify “the meetings,” though not in an abstract, but in a concrete sense (<hi type="italic">ecclesiae</hi>).<note placement="foot">It is doubtful whether the form מפעל (מפעל) is ever strictly a <hi type="italic">nomen actionis kal</hi> (Ges. §84, 14). Its meaning seems rather to be always concrete, even in Arabic, where <hi type="italic">menâm</hi> signifies a sleeping-place, sleeping-time, or a dream, but never sleep, or sleeping (like <hi type="italic">inse</hi>, Heb. <hi type="italic">shenâh</hi>, or <hi type="italic">naum</hi>, Heb. <hi type="italic">nūm</hi>).</note> <div eID="gen12846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12847" type="x-p"/> The explanatory clause, <hi type="italic">“for over all the glory</hi> (comes) <hi type="italic">a canopy,”</hi> admits of several interpretations. Dr. Shegg and others take it in the general sense: “for defence and covering are coming for all that is glorious.” Now, even if this thought were not so jejune as it is, the word <hi type="italic">Chuppâh</hi> would not be the word used to denote covering for the sake of protection; it signifies rather covering for the sake of beautifying and honouring that which is covered. <hi type="italic">Chuppâh</hi> is the name still given by the Jews to the wedding canopy, i.e., a canopy supported on four poles and carried by four boys, under which the bride and bridegroom receive the nuptial blessing - a meaning which is apparently more appropriate, even in <reference osisRef="Ps.19.6">Psa 19:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Joel.2.16">Joe 2:16</reference>, than the ordinary explanation <hi type="italic">thalamus</hi> to <hi type="italic">torus</hi>. Such a canopy would float above Mount Zion in the form of a cloud of smoke and blaze of fire. (There is no necessity to take <hi type="italic">Chuppâh</hi> as a third pers. <hi type="italic">pual</hi>, since תּהיה, which follows immediately afterwards in <reference osisRef="Isa.4.6">Isa 4:6</reference>, may easily be supplied in thought.) The only question is whether <hi type="italic">Col</hi> <hi type="italic">Câbōd</hi> signifies “every kind of glory,” or according to <reference osisRef="Ps.39.6">Psa 39:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.45.14">Psa 45:14</reference>, “pure glory” (Hofmann, <hi type="italic">Stud. u. Krit.</hi> 1847, pp. 936-38). The thought that Jerusalem would now be “all glory,” as its inhabitants were all holiness, and therefore that this shield would be spread out over pure glory, is one that thoroughly commends itself. but we nevertheless prefer the former, as more in accordance with the substantive clause. The glory which Zion would now possess would be exposed to no further injury: Jehovah would acknowledge it by signs of His gracious presence; for henceforth there would be nothing glorious in Zion, over which there would not be a canopy spread in the manner described, shading and yet enlightening, hiding, defending, and adorning it.
entries.6fa3377de9c976a9ae08959238361431b551bb45: <reference osisRef="Isa.4.6">Isa 4:6</reference> <div eID="gen12847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12848" type="x-p"/> Thus would Zion be a secure retreat from all adversities and disasters.<hi type="italic">"And it will be a booth for shade by day from the heat of the sun, and for a refuge and covert from storm and from rain.”</hi> The subject to <hi type="italic">“will be”</hi> is not the miraculous roofing; for <hi type="italic">ânân</hi> (cloud) is masculine, and the verb feminine, and there would be no sense in saying that a <hi type="italic">Chuppâh</hi> or canopy would be a <hi type="italic">succâh</hi> or booth. Either, therefore, the verb contains the subject in itself, and the meaning is, “There will be a booth” (the verb <hi type="italic">hâyâh</hi> being used in a pregnant sense, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.15.6">Isa 15:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.23.13">Isa 23:13</reference>); or else Zion (<reference osisRef="Isa.4.5">Isa 4:5</reference>) is the subject. We prefer the latter. Zion or Jerusalem would be a booth, that is to say, as the parallel clause affirms, a place of security and concealment (<hi type="italic">mistor</hi>, which only occurs here, is used on account of the alliteration with <hi type="italic">machseh</hi> in the place of <hi type="italic">sether</hi>, which the prophet more usually employs, viz., in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.17">Isa 28:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.2">Isa 32:2</reference>). <hi type="italic">“By day”</hi> (<hi type="italic">yōmâm</hi>, which is construed with לצל in the construct state, cf., <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.16">Eze 30:16</reference>) is left intentionally without any <hi type="italic">“by night”</hi> to answer to it in the parallel clause, because reference is made to a place of safety and concealment for all times, whether by day or night. Heat, storm, and rain are mentioned as examples to denote the most manifold dangers; but it is a singular fact that rain, which is a blessing so earnestly desired in the time of <hi type="italic">Chōreb</hi>, i.e., of drought and burning heat, should also be included. At the present day, when rain falls in Jerusalem, the whole city dances with delight. Nevertheless rain, i.e., the rain which falls from the clouds, is not paradisaical; and its effects are by no means unfrequently destructive. According to the archives of Genesis, rain from the clouds took the place of dew for the first time at the flood, when it fell in a continuous and destructive form. The Jerusalem of the last time will be paradise restored; and there men will be no longer exposed to destructive changes of weather. In this prediction the close of the prophetic discourse is linked on to the commencement. This mountain of Zion, roofed over with a cloud of smoke by day and the shining of a flaming fire by night, is no other than the mountain of the house of Jehovah, which was to be exalted above all the mountains, and to which the nations would make their pilgrimage; and this Jerusalem, so holy within, and all glorious without, is no other than the place from which the word of Jehovah was one day to go forth into all the world. But what Jerusalem is this? Is it the Jerusalem of the time of final glory awaiting the people of God in this life, as described in Rev 11 (for, notwithstanding all that a spiritualistic and rationalistic anti-chiliasm may say, the prophetic words of both Old and New Testament warrant us in expecting such a time of glory in this life); or is it the Jerusalem of the new heaven and new earth described in Rev 20:1-15 :21? The true answer is, “Both in one.” The prophet’s real intention was to depict the holy city in its final and imperishable state after the last judgment. But to his view, the state beyond and the closing state here were blended together, so that the glorified Jerusalem of earth and the glorified Jerusalem of heaven appeared as if fused into one. It was a distinguishing characteristic of the Old Testament, to represent the closing scene on this side the grave, and the eternal state beyond, as a continuous line, having its commencement here. The New Testament first drew the cross line which divides time from eternity. It is true, indeed, as the closing chapters of the Apocalypse show, that even the New Testament prophecies continue to some extent to depict the state beyond in figures drawn from the present world; with this difference, however, that when the line had once been drawn, the demand was made, of which there was no consciousness in the Old Testament, that the figures taken from this life should be understood as relating to the life beyond, and that eternal realities should be separated from their temporal forms.  <chapter eID="Isa.4"/> <div eID="gen12848" type="x-p"/>

entries.d847d0c7526d9e6d7519e815096f956ed6c6b0f5: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.4.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.4.1" sID="gen40888" type="section"/> <div sID="gen40889" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">In that day shall seven women take hold of one man</hi> He pursues the same subject, and unquestionably this discourse is immediately connected with what goes before. This verse certainly ought not to have been separated from the preceding. By this circumstance he describes more fully the nature of that desolation and calamity which he had formerly threatened against the Jews; for hypocrites; unless the threatening be conceived in strong terms, either disregard or palliate warnings, so that God’s severity never produces its proper effect upon them. From the effect, therefore, he describes the appalling nature of the approaching calamity, that they may not indulge the hope of making an easy escape. As if he had said, “Do not imagine that it will be of moderate extent, lessening your numbers in a small degree; for utter destruction awaits you, so that hardly <hi type="italic">one man</hi> will be found for <hi type="italic">seven women</hi>.”<div eID="gen40889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40890" type="x-p"/>The phrase <hi type="italic">take hold of</hi> conveys the same meaning. It is, no doubt, inconsistent with the modesty of the sex that a woman should, of her own accord, offer herself to a man. But the Prophet says, that not only will they do this, but that <hi type="italic">seven women</hi> will, as it were, lay hands on a man, and keep hold of him; so small will be the number of men. The greatness of the calamity is likewise denoted by what immediately follows: <hi type="italic">we will eat our own bread, and wear our own apparel</hi>; for as it is a duty which belongs to a husband to support his wife and family, the women ask a husband for themselves on unreasonable conditions, when they release him from all concern about supplying them with food. Very great must, therefore, be the scarcity of men, when a great number of women, laying aside modesty, are not only constrained to solicit one man, but do not even shrink from the agreement to procure their own victuals, and request nothing more from a husband than to receive them within the bond of marriage.<div eID="gen40890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40891" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Let thy name be called on us.</hi> It may be rendered, <hi type="italic">Let us be</hi> <hi type="italic">called by thy name</hi>; for when a woman passes into the family of her husband, she is <hi type="italic">called by his name</hi>, and loses her own, because the husband is her head. (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.11.3">1 Corinthians 11:3</reference>.) Hence the vail is a token of subjection, and Abimelech said to Sarah,<div eID="gen40891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40892" type="x-p"/>Thy husband Abraham shall be a covering to thy head. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.20.16">Genesis 20:16</reference>.)<div eID="gen40892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40893" type="x-p"/>But if she remain unmarried, she is concealed under the name of her family. That this is the true meaning of that mode of expression is sufficiently evident from what Jacob says when blessing his grandchildren,<div eID="gen40893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40894" type="x-p"/>Let my name, and the name of my fathers, <lb/> Abraham and Isaac, be called on them; (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.48.16">Genesis 48:16</reference>;)<div eID="gen40894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40895" type="x-p"/>that is, “Let them be reckoned as our descendants, and let them be partakers of the covenant, and never excluded from it, as were Esau and Ishmael.” In the same manner also do heathen writers speak; as, in Lucan, Marcia, wishing to return to Cato, says: “Grant me only the bare name of marriage; let permission be given that it may be inscribed on my tomb, Marcia the wife of Cato.” <note n="70"> <div sID="gen40896" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="la">Da tantum nomen inane Connubii: liceat tumulo scripsisse, Catonis Marcia</foreign>. Luc. Phars. 2:342.<div eID="gen40896" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen40895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40897" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And take away our reproach.</hi> Their reason for saying so is, that women are sometimes treated with disdain, when they do not obtain husbands, not only because they appear to be despised as unworthy, but because among the ancient people offspring was reckoned an important blessing, and therefore the Prophet says that they will be desirous to wipe away this reproach, and will employ every argument for that purpose. Lastly, he declares that the calamity will be so great, that almost all the men will be carried off.<div eID="gen40897" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.4.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen40888" osisID="Isa.4.1" type="section"/>
entries.6b9b03052a981ab1a383701ce7d2f24ecbed527e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.4.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.4.2" sID="gen40898" type="section"/> <div sID="gen40899" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2.</hi> <hi type="italic">In that day shall the branch of the Lord be for beauty and glory.</hi> <note n="71"> <div sID="gen40900" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic"> In that day shall the branch of the Lord be beautiful and</hi> <hi type="italic">glorious</hi>. — Eng. Ver. The marginal reading is, <hi type="italic">beauty and glory</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen40900" type="x-p"/> </note> This consolation is seasonably added; for the announcement of a dreadful calamity might have alarmed the godly, and led them to doubt as to the stability of God’s covenant being maintained amidst the destruction of the people. For there is a wide difference between the two statements, that the people will be <hi type="italic">like the sand of the sea</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.22.17">Genesis 22:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.10.22">Isaiah 10:22</reference>,) and yet that they would be cut down by such a frightful massacre, that in the remnant there would be found no dignity, no magnificence, and hardly any name. Isaiah, therefore, according to the custom generally followed by himself and by the prophets, provides against this alarm, and, by adding a consolation, assuages their excessive terror, that believers may still rest assured that the Church will be safe, and may strengthen their hearts by good hope.
